questions.question: Explain how deindividuation can lead to both antisocial and prosocial behaviour in crowds.

points.text: Deindividuation reduces personal accountability - people follow group norms. In an antisocial crowd (riot), anonymity leads to aggression because the group norm is destructive. In a prosocial crowd (charity run), anonymity leads to helpfulness because the group norm is supportive.

questions.question: Describe Tajfel's minimal group paradigm and evaluate what it tells us about prejudice.

points.text: Tajfel showed that even arbitrary group divisions create in-group favouritism. This demonstrates that prejudice arises from the basic cognitive process of categorisation. Limitation: the paradigm is artificial - real-world prejudice involves history, power, and material conflict.

questions.question: Evaluate methods for reducing prejudice, referring to psychological research.

points.text: Contact hypothesis: prejudice reduces when groups interact under equal status, cooperation, and shared goals. Sherif's Robbers Cave: hostile groups reconciled when they worked together on superordinate goals. Evaluation: contact works under optimal conditions but may backfire if groups compete.

questions.question: Full-Mark Response Evaluate the view that prejudice is an inevitable consequence of group membership. <div class="

points.text: A grade 9 response will: explain SIT (categorisation creates in-group favouritism automatically); support with Tajfel's minimal group paradigm; evaluate (SIT shows bias is basic to group membership); counter-argument (prejudice levels vary across cultures and time, contact reduces prejudice, superordinate goals create cooperation); conclude: while the cognitive processes are basic, the expression of prejudice is not inevitable - it depends on social context and whether conditions promote intergroup contact.
